title: What Is Strategy?
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, year, journal, volume 74, issue 6 and pages 61–78 matched in a university course listing and a library bibliography; an article index summarized the same central argument. The hbr.org address is HBR’s archive address for the November 1996 issue; it was not returned in search results and the link was not opened.

summary: Porter argues that operational effectiveness — performing similar activities better than rivals — is necessary but not sufficient for superior performance, because its techniques diffuse and competitors converge. Strategy is the creation of a unique and valuable position, rooted in a system of activities, which requires trade-offs and fit among those activities. Choosing what not to do is, in his account, the essence of strategy.
arguments: Operational effectiveness is not strategy: best practices spread, producing competitive convergence.
Positions can rest on the variety of products served, the needs of a customer group, or differences in access to customers.
A position is sustainable only with trade-offs; rivals that copy without accepting them end up straddling.
Fit among activities makes a strategy hard to imitate because rivals must copy a system, not a practice.
design: Conceptual essay illustrated with company examples; no systematic data or statistical test.
strengths: Exceptionally clear conceptual distinctions (operational effectiveness vs. positioning, trade-offs, fit) that remain the reference point for strategy teaching; the argument is precise enough to be used as a test of real plans.
limitations: Evidence is illustrative and drawn from successful firms, so survivorship and hindsight bias are possible; it says little about how positions should change when technology moves the productivity frontier quickly.
contested: Mintzberg and Waters’ emergent view (R-mintzberg-1985-strategies) challenges the emphasis on deliberate design; critics of static positioning argue that fast-moving markets erode positions quickly. These are disagreements about emphasis and setting rather than failed replications.
generalizability: The logic transfers well to any organization competing for customers, talent or funding, including public agencies and sports organizations; the specific examples are commercial.
relevance: Gives you the sharpest available test of whether a departmental or organizational plan is a strategy or a list of improvements, and why “what we will stop doing” belongs in every plan.

title: Good Strategy Bad Strategy: The Difference and Why It Matters
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, publisher (Crown Business, New York), year 2011 and ISBN 9780307886231 matched in library catalogue records and the Penguin Random House listing. The kernel (diagnosis, guiding policy, coherent action) and the hallmarks of bad strategy were confirmed from multiple secondary summaries, not from the book text.

summary: Rumelt distinguishes good strategy from the goals, slogans and wish lists that often pass for it. A good strategy has a kernel: a diagnosis that names the critical challenge, a guiding policy for dealing with it, and coherent actions that carry the policy out. He catalogues the hallmarks of bad strategy, including fluff, failure to face the challenge, mistaking goals for strategy and poorly chosen strategic objectives.
arguments: The kernel of a strategy is diagnosis, guiding policy and coherent action.
Goals and aspirations are not strategies; a strategy explains how a specific obstacle will be overcome.
Bad strategy is common and recognizable: fluff, failure to face the challenge, goals mistaken for strategy, and jumbled or unattainable objectives.
Good strategy concentrates resources and action where they will have the greatest effect.
design: Book-length argument drawing on the author’s consulting and teaching experience and on business and historical examples; no systematic empirical test.
strengths: Highly practical; the kernel can be applied at any level, from a whole company to a single department, and makes weak plans easy to spot.
limitations: A practitioner framework built from experience and selected examples; there is no evidence that plans containing a kernel outperform others, and examples are chosen by the author.
generalizability: Applies broadly to business, government, military and sports organizations; best used as a diagnostic checklist rather than as a predictive model.
relevance: Provides the template for this week’s strategy memo and a language for challenging plans that confuse ambition with strategy.

title: Of Strategies, Deliberate and Emergent
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 6, issue 3 and pages 257–272 matched on RePEc/IDEAS and EconPapers. The DOI was seen on the publisher’s download stamp of a copy in search results, not on the Wiley landing page.

summary: Mintzberg and Waters distinguish intended strategies (what leaders plan) from realized strategies (the patterns that actually appear in an organization’s actions). Deliberate and emergent strategies are two ends of a continuum along which real strategies lie, and the authors describe intermediate types such as planned, entrepreneurial, ideological, umbrella, process, unconnected, consensus and imposed strategies.
arguments: Strategy can be a pattern in a stream of actions, not only a plan.
Intended strategies may be realized (deliberate) or unrealized; emergent strategies are realized patterns that were never intended.
Purely deliberate and purely emergent strategies are rare; most lie between them.
Emergent strategy allows organizational learning; deliberate strategy provides direction and control.
design: Conceptual paper proposing a continuum and a typology of strategies.
strengths: Changes how you read an organization: look at what it does and funds, not only at what it says. Widely used and conceptually durable.
limitations: A typology rather than a tested theory; classifying a strategy as emergent or deliberate is often done after the fact.
contested: Stands in a long-running debate with design and positioning views of strategy (e.g. R-porter-1996-what) about how much strategy should be planned; the debate concerns emphasis, not replication.
generalizability: Applies to any organization; especially useful where front-line staff make many decisions that add up to a strategy, as in hospitals, consulting firms and player development.
relevance: Supports the week’s central practical point: an organization’s real strategy is visible in its resource allocation.

title: The Five Competitive Forces That Shape Strategy
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, January 2008 issue, volume 86, issue 1 matched on the HBR Store (product R0801E) and a library catalogue; pages given as 78–93 in one citation and 79–93 in another catalogue. Confirmed as an update of Porter’s 1979 HBR article.

summary: Porter restates and extends his 1979 framework: industry profitability is shaped by the threat of new entrants, the bargaining power of suppliers and buyers, the threat of substitutes and the intensity of rivalry. The strongest forces determine how much of the value an industry creates its firms can keep. He distinguishes these forces from factors such as growth, technology, government and complements, which matter through the forces, and describes common errors in applying the framework.
arguments: Five forces shape the long-run average profitability of an industry.
The strongest force or forces matter most and differ by industry.
Growth, technology, government and complementary products are factors, not forces.
Good strategy positions a firm where the forces are weakest, exploits changes in them, or reshapes them.
design: Conceptual article grounded in industrial-organization economics, with industry illustrations.
strengths: A durable, widely taught structure for analyzing why industries differ in profitability; the 2008 version addresses common misapplications.
limitations: Largely static; treats buyers and suppliers mainly as bargaining threats; handles platforms, ecosystems and cooperation only indirectly.
contested: Variance-decomposition studies disagree on how much industry explains relative to firm-specific factors (R-mcgahan-1997-much; R-barney-1991-firm offers the firm-level counterpoint).
generalizability: Works best for commercial industries with identifiable products and rivals; applying it to sports leagues, public services or platforms requires care in defining the industry.
relevance: Teaches you to ask who captures the value an activity creates, which matters for any organization buying talent, technology or services.

title: Value-based Business Strategy
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 5, issue 1, pages 5–24 and DOI matched on EconPapers (RePEc) and Scilit; the abstract’s main points (definition of value, added value, asymmetries, four value-based strategies, cooperative game theory) appeared in the same records.

summary: Brandenburger and Stuart define the value created in a vertical chain as buyers’ willingness to pay minus suppliers’ opportunity cost, and a firm’s added value as the value lost if the firm were removed. Using cooperative game theory, they argue that added value limits how much value a firm can capture, and that positive added value requires asymmetries between a firm and its rivals. The analysis gives supplier and buyer relationships equal weight.
arguments: Value created equals willingness to pay minus suppliers’ opportunity cost.
A firm’s added value caps the value it can capture.
Positive added value requires an asymmetry between the firm and its competitors.
Strategies can work on the supplier side as well as the buyer side.
design: Formal conceptual analysis based on cooperative game theory.
strengths: Precise definitions that separate value creation from value capture and make cooperation as analyzable as competition.
limitations: Abstract; real willingness-to-pay and opportunity-cost figures are hard to measure, and the bound on capture depends on modelling assumptions.
generalizability: Transfers well to procurement, hiring and partnership decisions in any sector, including the competition for players, coaches and analysts.
relevance: Gives you a rigorous way to ask “what do we add that others cannot?” before negotiating price, salary or partnership terms.

title: How Much Does Industry Matter, Really?
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 18, supplement issue S1 (July 1997) and pages 15–30 matched on RePEc/IDEAS and EconPapers, which also report the variance shares cited in the lesson. The DOI string appeared garbled in results, so it is omitted.

summary: McGahan and Porter decompose the variance in business-unit profitability into year, industry, corporate-parent and business-specific effects. They report that industry effects account for roughly 19% of the variance and business-specific effects for roughly 32%, with smaller corporate-parent (about 4%) and year (about 2%) effects. Industry effects were smaller in manufacturing and larger in service sectors such as lodging and entertainment, wholesale and retail trade, and transportation.
arguments: Both industry and business-specific effects explain meaningful shares of profitability differences.
Business-specific effects are larger on average than industry effects.
The importance of industry varies by sector: lower in manufacturing, higher in several service sectors.
Corporate-parent and industry effects covary negatively across sectors.
design: Variance-components decomposition of business-unit profitability across U.S. industries.
strengths: Large-sample evidence on a question that strategy frameworks often answer by assertion; reports sector differences rather than a single number.
limitations: Descriptive, not causal; the business-specific share is partly a residual that includes luck and measurement differences; results depend on industry definitions, period and method.
contested: Other variance-decomposition studies report different splits between industry and firm effects depending on sample and method; resource-based scholars (R-barney-1991-firm) read the larger firm share as support for firm-level explanations, while positioning scholars stress the industry share.
generalizability: Concerns U.S. commercial business units; transfer to sports leagues or public organizations is by analogy only.
relevance: Shows how to weigh “where we compete” against “how well we compete” with evidence, and how to read a variance share without over-interpreting it.

title: Firm Resources and Sustained Competitive Advantage
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, journal, volume 17, issue 1, pages 99–120, publisher (SAGE) and DOI matched on BibBase, Scilit and CiNii; abstract content (value, rareness, imitability, substitutability) confirmed in the same records.

summary: Barney builds the resource-based view on two assumptions — strategic resources are heterogeneous across firms and imperfectly mobile — and proposes that resources can generate sustained competitive advantage when they are valuable, rare, imperfectly imitable and not strategically substitutable. He explains imperfect imitability through unique historical conditions, causal ambiguity and social complexity.
arguments: Sustained advantage requires resource heterogeneity and immobility.
Valuable, rare, imperfectly imitable and non-substitutable resources can sustain advantage.
History, causal ambiguity and social complexity make resources hard to imitate.
Resources that can be bought on open markets rarely create sustained advantage.
design: Conceptual article that derives conditions for sustained advantage and applies them to several kinds of resources.
strengths: Foundational and highly cited; turns attention from industries to what is inside the firm; the VRIN criteria are easy to apply.
limitations: Key resources are hard to observe and measure; the criteria are easier to apply after success than before it.
contested: Priem and Butler (R-priem-2001-is) argued that the framework is close to tautological and neglects how resource value is set in product markets; Barney replied in the same journal issue that the direct criticisms were unfounded.
generalizability: Transfers well to professional services, healthcare, the military and sports organizations, where much of what matters is people, routines and relationships.
relevance: Explains why buying the same technology as rivals cannot by itself create an edge, and where to look for one instead.

title: Is the Resource-Based “View” a Useful Perspective for Strategic Management Research?
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 26, issue 1 and pages 22–40 matched on EconBiz, Scilit-linked records and reference lists on journals.aom.org. Search results gave conflicting DOIs, so the DOI is omitted and the EconBiz catalogue record is used as the link.

summary: Priem and Butler argue that the resource-based view, as then formulated, is not yet a theoretical structure. They contend that it risks tautology when valuable resources are defined by the advantage they are meant to explain, that it assumed stable product markets, and that it did not explain how resource value is determined. They outline challenges for improving it, including formalization and integration with demand-side considerations.
arguments: The elemental RBV is at risk of being true by definition rather than testable.
Resource value is determined outside the firm, in product markets, which the RBV had not addressed.
The RBV had assumed stable product markets and paid little attention to time.
The framework needs formalization and integration with models of demand.
design: Critical conceptual review of the resource-based literature.
strengths: Forces precision about what counts as a valuable resource; its demand-side point remains influential.
limitations: A critique of theory construction rather than an empirical test; supporters dispute how much of the critique applies to Barney’s 1991 framework.
contested: Barney replied in the same issue (Academy of Management Review 26(1), 41–56) that the direct criticisms of his 1991 article were unfounded, while acknowledging the requirements the critique highlighted; Priem and Butler’s further comments in the same issue (pp. 57–66) reaffirmed the tautology charge for the elemental business-level RBV. See R-barney-1991-firm.
generalizability: The lesson — define value from customers and costs, before the fact — applies to any organization judging its own strengths.
relevance: Protects you from the most common misuse of strategy frameworks: labelling whatever a winner has as the cause of its winning.

title: Dynamic Capabilities and Strategic Management
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 18, issue 7, pages 509–533 (August 1997) matched on RePEc/IDEAS and EconPapers; the DOI appeared in full in a reference list and garbled on RePEc (an angle-bracket rendering problem). The definition of dynamic capabilities (p. 516) was confirmed from search-result excerpts.

summary: Teece, Pisano and Shuen propose the dynamic capabilities framework: a firm’s ability to integrate, build and reconfigure internal and external competences to address rapidly changing environments. They argue that competitive advantage rests on the firm’s organizational and managerial processes, shaped by its asset positions and by the paths available to it.
arguments: In fast-changing markets, the ability to reconfigure competences matters more than any fixed resource.
Advantage depends on processes, positions and paths.
Capabilities are path-dependent: what a firm can do next depends on what it has learned.
Many valuable capabilities cannot be bought; they must be built.
design: Conceptual framework contrasting dynamic capabilities with other approaches to strategy.
strengths: Extends the resource-based view to changing environments and explains why organizational learning and reconfiguration matter.
limitations: Concepts are broad and hard to measure; there is a risk of identifying dynamic capabilities by the successful adaptation they are meant to explain.
contested: Shares the tautology concern raised against the resource-based view (R-priem-2001-is) when capabilities are inferred from outcomes.
generalizability: Useful for any organization facing technological change, including healthcare systems and sports organizations adopting new measurement technology.
relevance: Shifts attention from owning the best tools to being able to rebuild routines as tools and markets change.

title: An Economic Evaluation of the Moneyball Hypothesis
license: Copyright holder’s terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, journal, volume 20, issue 3, pages 173–186 and DOI matched on EconPapers (RePEc) and EconBiz; findings (data 1999–2004; on-base percentage undervalued before the book; undervaluation diminished after publication) matched in multiple summaries. The American Economic Association distributes JEP articles free online; one search summary described the article as paywalled, so access should be checked when the link is first opened.

summary: Hakes and Sauer test Michael Lewis’s claim that baseball’s labor market mispriced certain skills. Using standard econometric methods on player productivity and compensation data from 1999 to 2004, they find that a hitter’s on-base percentage was undervalued relative to its contribution to winning before the book appeared, and that the undervaluation diminished after its publication.
arguments: Market inefficiencies in a professional labor market can be measured with standard econometric tools.
On-base skill was undervalued relative to its contribution to winning before the book was published.
The mispricing narrowed after the idea became public, consistent with arbitrage eroding the edge.
design: Regression analysis of team winning and player salaries using major-league data, 1999–2004.
strengths: Clear, testable question; transparent methods; one of the few empirical tests of a famous business story; a later honors thesis reported replicating the main regressions.
limitations: Observational, short post-publication window, and sensitive to model specification; publication of the book is one of several possible channels for the correction.
contested: The paper prompted public debate, including the argument that the featured club’s success owed more to pitching than to on-base skill. A 2020 University of Vermont honors thesis reported reproducing the regressions and cross-validating them with an agent-based model (not in the library).
generalizability: The mechanism — information-based edges eroding once visible — generalizes well to finance, retail and talent markets; the specific estimates apply to that period of the baseball labor market only.
relevance: Directly relevant evidence on how quickly an analytical edge in a sports labor market can be competed away, and why advantage must be renewed.
